screens.title: Backup & Restore DR with AWS Backup and Amazon S3
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how the Backup and Restore disaster recovery model uses managed backups and durable storage to protect data while keeping costs reasonable. We'll focus on AWS Backup as a centralized service that schedules, encrypts, and copies backups across Regions, and on Amazon S3 for storing durable objects with versioning and object lock. You will see practical configuration ideas: how to define backup rules, retention and lifecycle policies, assign resources by tag, and create cross-Region copies so that a catastrophic Region failure does not destroy your recovery points. We also cover S3 features like versioning and cross-Region replication to keep offsite object copies, and how to run a simulated restore to validate your runbook. A common risk to watch for is thinking a backup exists because a snapshot was taken; without the right IAM permissions, lifecycle rules, or tested restores, that backup may be unusable. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to design a backup plan that balances RTO and RPO needs, use S3 for durable offsite copies, and run a restore test to prove recovery. Consider what recovery time you can tolerate and how often you must copy backups to another Region before we begin.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure centralized backup plans, optimize retention and lifecycle to control cost, and use Amazon S3 features to protect object data. First, you'll define backup rules and vaults in AWS Backup so multiple services follow a single policy. Second, you'll implement schedules, retention and lifecycle to balance storage costs against recovery needs; this matters because long retention without lifecycle transitions increases expense. Third, you will enable S3 versioning and object lock so object histories are preserved and protected from accidental deletes or ransomware—this is essential for compliance and recovery. Lastly, you'll configure S3 Cross-Region Replication and AWS Backup cross-Region copy so recovery points are stored offsite. Each objective is practical: for example, assigning EC2 instances to a backup plan by tag ensures systems added later inherit the same protection automatically. A typical misconception is assuming a backup alone guarantees recovery; instead, you must test simulated restores and validate integrity. These skills let you design cost-effective, auditable backup policies that your team can rely on during a disaster. Which objective feels most urgent for your environment today?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: This screen translates objectives into practical tasks you can perform. You'll create an AWS Backup plan with a daily schedule and retention policy, assign EC2 and RDS resources by tag, and add a cross-Region copy to a secondary Region. You'll also enable versioning on an S3 bucket and configure Cross-Region Replication, then upload and verify a sample object replicates. The reason these tasks matter is they translate policy into repeatable actions: tags ensure new instances are automatically backed up, replication keeps offsite copies without manual transfers, and test restores confirm that the whole system works. A common misconception is treating replication and backup as identical; replication is for object copies while AWS Backup handles snapshots and cross-Region backup copies at the service level. As you practice, pay attention to required IAM roles and encryption settings — both are common causes of failed backups or replication. These tasks will prepare you for the lab where you launch a small EC2, attach tags, create a backup plan, and verify cross-Region copies and S3 replication.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Applied Tasks

Practical checklist

Step-by-step tasks to practice core backup and S3 operations.

1. Launch a tagged EC2 instance and verify tags.
2. Create an AWS Backup plan: daily schedule, 7-day retention, cross-Region copy.
3. Assign resources by tag to the backup plan.

Quick warnings & tips

Tip: Use tags for consistent selection and fewer manual steps.
Warning: Missing IAM role for AWS Backup or S3 replication will block operations.
Validation: Always run a simulated restore into a test environment and update runbooks with the results.

screens.title: Backup & Restore DR model — definition and trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Backup and Restore is a disaster recovery model where you create recovery points in storage and restore systems and data only after an outage. It typically has longer recovery time objectives and recovery point objectives than warm standby or pilot light models, but it is often the most cost-efficient option for systems that can tolerate delays. Practically, this means you plan for longer downtime but benefit from lower ongoing costs because you do not maintain running standby infrastructure. For example, a non-critical batch processing application that runs once per day often uses Backup and Restore: nightly snapshots and S3 backups will let you recover within hours rather than minutes. A common misconception is assuming backups eliminate the need for testing. In reality, a backup is not useful unless you can restore it; therefore simulated restores and runbook validation are essential. Another contrast: replication and high-availability designs aim for minimal downtime, while Backup and Restore focuses on data durability and cost. The takeaway is to match recovery tolerances to business needs, and then design backup schedules, retention, and offsite copies to meet those tolerances while keeping costs under control. What recovery window does your application require, and does that match a Backup and Restore strategy?

keyIdea.text: Backup & Restore trades faster recovery for lower cost; use it when longer RTO/RPO are acceptable and validate restores regularly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Backup & Restore Model
Definition

Backup and Restore explained

Create recovery points, store them durably, and restore systems when needed. Best for workloads that tolerate longer downtime.

Example: Nightly backups for a daily analytics job; recovery within hours is acceptable.
Why it matters: Lower cost because you don't run redundant systems, you only store recovery points.
Misconception: A snapshot exists so recovery is guaranteed — without tested restores and correct IAM, it may fail.
Process snapshot
Match RTO and RPO to business needs, then choose backup frequency and retention. Add cross-Region copies to protect against regional failure.
Key takeaway
Backup & Restore is cost-effective but requires routine restore validation to ensure recoverability.
Check your understanding
Which applications in your environment can tolerate longer RTOs, and which cannot?

screens.title: AWS Backup — centralized service and supported resources
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Backup is a fully managed service that centralizes backup operations across a range of AWS services. It supports EC2 snapshots, EBS volumes, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx and Storage Gateway volumes. Centralization matters because it frees teams from maintaining separate scripts for each service and enables consistent policy enforcement. For example, rather than creating separate retention scripts for each database, you define one backup plan with rules and apply it to all targets. This simplifies audits and enforces consistency. A typical setup includes a backup vault where snapshots are stored, often encrypted using a customer-managed key. You should be aware of roles: AWS Backup requires an IAM role with permissions to create snapshots and manage lifecycle; forgetting to attach the correct role is a common operational mistake. Another useful capability is copying backups to another Region automatically. This cross-Region copy is not the same as S3 replication; it's a managed copy of a backup recovery point. Finally, centralization also helps with reporting and compliance because backup activity appears in a single place. Practice: create a simple backup plan that targets EC2 and RDS to see these benefits play out in one policy.

keyIdea.title: AWS Backup
keyIdea.text: Centralizes backups for many AWS services, simplifying policy management and auditability while enabling encryption and cross-Region copies.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › AWS Backup
Supported resources

One service, many targets

Services supported include EC2 snapshots, EBS volumes, Amazon RDS, DynamoDB tables, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, and AWS Storage Gateway volumes.
Centralization simplifies policy enforcement, auditing, and lifecycle management across these resource types.
Example
Define a single backup plan that schedules daily snapshots for both RDS and EC2 instances tagged as Production so new instances inherit protection automatically.
Operational notes
Use a backup vault for storage and encryption, and ensure AWS Backup has the IAM role it needs to manage snapshots. Without the role, backups will fail.
Benefit
Consistent backups across services and simplified compliance reporting.
Common mistake
Not assigning the correct IAM role to AWS Backup, preventing snapshots and copy actions.

screens.title: Designing a Backup Plan — rules, window, retention, lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a backup plan starts with translating RTO and RPO into concrete rules: how often to take backups and how long to keep them. Begin by choosing a schedule expression that aligns with recovery point needs. For example, if you need hourly recovery points, schedule hourly backups; if daily is sufficient, choose a daily cron. Next, set a backup window that sets the preferred time to start backups to reduce load during peak hours. Then decide retention: short retention for frequent restores, longer retention for compliance. Finally, add lifecycle rules to transition older backups to colder storage for cost savings, such as moving snapshots to archival storage after thirty days. A cross-Region copy can be added as a copy action with its own retention to isolate recovery points. An example pattern is: daily backups, 7-day primary retention, cross-Region copy retained 30 days, and lifecycle transition to archive after 60 days. Remember a frequent mistake: setting very short start windows that cannot complete given the completion window — this can cause overlapping jobs. Validate your times against expected snapshot durations and adjust start and completion windows accordingly. The practical exercise is to convert your RTO/RPO requirements into these rule fields and test a manual restore.

keyIdea.title: Backup Plan Design
keyIdea.text: Map RTO/RPO to schedule, choose an appropriate backup window, set retention, and use lifecycle rules and cross-Region copy to balance cost and resilience.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Backup Plan Design
Process

From RTO/RPO to backup rules

1. Schedule
Choose cron or daily expressions to meet RPO requirements.
2. Backup Window
Pick a start window that avoids peak load and allows completion.
3. Retention
Set retention to meet recovery and compliance needs.
4. Lifecycle & Copy Actions
Transition older backups to colder storage and add cross-Region copies for offsite durability.
Concrete example
Daily backups at 05:00 UTC, StartWindow 60 minutes, CompletionWindow 180 minutes, Retain 35 days. Cross-Region copy retained 365 days and lifecycle transition to archival after 90 days.
Common mistake
Not accounting for backup duration and causing overlapping jobs that can fail or extend past completion windows.
Key takeaway
Translate service-level RTO/RPO to concrete schedule, windows, retention and lifecycle settings, then test them.

screens.title: Assigning resources to a backup plan using tags
screens.narratorSegment: Assigning resources by tag is a practical and scalable way to ensure new resources inherit backup protection. In AWS Backup, create a backup selection that targets specific resource types and includes conditions where a tag key equals a tag value, for example Environment equals Production. This minimizes manual selection and adapts to infrastructure that grows over time. Behind the scenes AWS Backup needs an IAM role that allows it to take snapshots and manage backups; the role must be provided in the backup selection call. A frequent operational pitfall is forgetting to set the IAM role in the selection, which prevents AWS Backup from accessing specified resources. Another consideration is resource type differences: some services, like RDS, have snapshot semantics different from EBS volume snapshots, so verify your selection covers the intended resource types. For example, assign EC2 and RDS resources to the same plan by specifying both resource types and the matching tag condition to ensure consistent retention. After assignment, trigger a manual run to confirm backups succeed and inspect the backup vault to confirm encryption and copy actions are present. This approach keeps policy enforcement declarative and repeatable.

keyIdea.title: Resource assignment
keyIdea.text: Use tags and backup selections to automatically include resources in a backup plan and ensure the correct IAM role is specified for backup operations.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Resource Assignment
How-to

Assign resources by tag

Create a backup selection with Conditions where a tag key equals a value. Include resource types like EC2 and RDS to cover different services within the same plan.
CLI example (concept)
aws backup put-backup-selection --backup-plan-id "backup-plan-id" --backup-selection '{
  "SelectionName": "ProdSelection",
  "IamRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/service-role/AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole",
  "Resources": [
    {
      "ResourceType": "EC2",
      "Conditions": { "StringEquals": { "ConditionKey": "Environment", "ConditionValue": "Production" } }
    },
    {
      "ResourceType": "RDS",
      "Conditions": { "StringEquals": { "ConditionKey": "Application", "ConditionValue": "WebApp" } }
    }
  ]
}'
Checklist
Confirm IAM role has snapshot and tagging read permissions.
Run a manual backup to verify resource selection and vault storage.
If backups fail, inspect CloudTrail and IAM role policies first.

screens.title: Backup Vaults, Encryption and Lifecycle management
screens.narratorSegment: A backup vault is a logical container where AWS Backup stores recovery points. Vaults are often encrypted using AWS KMS keys and are the primary boundary for access control and lifecycle management. Using vaults helps you separate environments or compliance categories; for instance you might store production backups in a vault with stricter encryption keys and longer retention. Lifecycle rules attached to backup rules let you transition backups to cheaper storage tiers after a period, reducing ongoing cost. For example, you can retain a snapshot in the primary vault for 35 days and then transition it to an archive tier or cross-Region copy retained for 365 days, depending on compliance needs. A common operational oversight is failing to set the correct KMS key grants for cross-Region copies—if the destination cannot decrypt, the copy will be unusable. Always validate encryption and IAM permissions for both the source and destination vaults. Finally, document vault usage and lifecycle policies so your team understands where to look for a recovery point, and automate reporting so that retention rules are enforced consistently. The core outcome is encrypted, auditable backup storage that also optimizes cost through lifecycle transitions.

keyIdea.title: Vault & lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Use backup vaults with KMS encryption and lifecycle transitions to secure backups and reduce costs through staged retention.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Vaults & Lifecycles
Vaults

Secure and organize backups

Vaults act as containers for recovery points and control encryption and access boundaries. Use separate vaults for differing compliance or retention requirements.
Example
Production vault with KMS key A and 90-day retention; archive copies retained in a different vault with longer retention and separate key.
Lifecycle

Transition to colder storage

Lifecycle rules let you move backups to archival storage or delete them after a defined period. This reduces cost while preserving long-term recovery points when required.
Ensure KMS grants exist for cross-Region copies, or copies may be unreadable in the destination vault.
Key takeaway: Combine vaults, encryption and lifecycle to meet both security and cost requirements.

screens.title: AWS Backup Cross-Region Copy
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-Region copy in AWS Backup automatically copies a recovery point to a specified destination Region and backup vault. This protects against a Region-wide outage by keeping an independent, isolated copy of your backup outside the primary Region. You configure copy actions within a backup rule, specifying the destination vault ARN and lifecycle settings for the copy. For example, a daily backup can be copied to us-west-2 with a separate retention schedule of one year. One important operational detail: cross-Region copies use KMS-encrypted vaults, so ensure the destination key grants decryption permissions as needed and that roles permit copy actions. Cross-Region copy differs from S3 CRR: AWS Backup copies snapshots and recovery points for multiple resource types, whereas S3 CRR replicates objects between buckets. A common misconception is expecting instantaneous copies; cross-Region copies are asynchronous and depend on snapshot size and service throttling. After enabling cross-Region copy, inspect the destination vault to confirm the copied recovery points appear and perform a test restore from the copied recovery point into a DR test account or Region to confirm integrity and permissions. AWS Backup Cross-Region Copy means use aws backup's cross-region copy action to place recovery points in an isolated region and verify kms and iam permissions for usability.. In practical terms, protect recovery points by copying backups to another aws region. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Cross-Region Copy
What it does

Copy recovery points across Regions

Add copy actions to backup rules to replicate recovery points to a destination vault in another Region and apply retention specific to the copy.
Example rule snippet
"CopyActions": [
  {
    "DestinationBackupVaultArn": "arn:aws:backup:us-west-2:123456789012:backup-vault:Default",
    "Lifecycle": { "DeleteAfterDays": 365 }
  }
]
Operational notes
Cross-Region copies are asynchronous and require KMS grants and appropriate IAM roles. Validate that copies appear in the destination vault and that you can restore from them during testing.
Key takeaway: Cross-Region copy ensures isolation of recovery points from a single Region failure.
Common mistake: Not granting the destination KMS key the right permission prevents decryption of copied recovery points.

screens.title: Amazon S3 for backups — durability, versioning, and object lock
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon S3 provides a durable and scalable object store suitable for storing backup data, logs, and configuration files. Its eleven nines of durability dramatically reduces the chance of object loss, making it a strong option for backup storage. Key S3 features for DR include versioning, which keeps multiple versions of an object so you can recover an earlier state after accidental deletion or overwrite. Object Lock provides write-once-read-many (WORM) protections to prevent deletion or modification for a defined retention period, which is valuable for regulatory compliance and ransomware protection. When using these features together you get both the ability to recover previous object versions and the assurance that a retention policy cannot be bypassed. However, enabling Object Lock and versioning requires planning because object lifecycles and replication behave differently when versions and locks are present. Cost is another factor: keeping many versions or large objects across Regions increases storage charges. Always balance protection needs against cost and operational complexity, and document S3 lifecycle, retention, and lock policies so teams understand how to recover object histories when needed. Durability

S3 durability and storage

S3 offers high durability for backups and is suited for object storage, including logs and archived configuration files. Consider storage class choices when planning cost and retrieval time.
Versioning & Object Lock

Protect object history

Enable versioning to preserve prior object states. Enable object lock for WORM-style protection to prevent deletion or modification for a retention period.
CLI reminder
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket my-source-bucket --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
Key takeaway
Versioning plus object lock provides recoverability and regulatory protection, but plan lifecycle and cost implications before enabling both.

screens.title: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR)
screens.narratorSegment: S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies objects from a source bucket in one AWS Region to a destination bucket in another Region. CRR is configured at the bucket level and requires versioning enabled on both source and destination buckets, plus an IAM role that allows replication. After enabling CRR, new objects and updates (when configured) are asynchronously replicated to the destination. This creates an offsite copy suitable for DR scenarios where object availability in another Region is needed. An example workflow is: enable versioning on both buckets, create the destination bucket, add a replication rule that targets all objects or a specific prefix, and create or grant the replication role. In practice, replication is not instantaneous; it is asynchronous and may take time depending on object size and throughput. Consider costs: storing replicated objects in another Region increases storage costs and potential egress on large-scale recovery. A common misconception is thinking replication replaces backups: replication copies objects but does not take consistent multi-resource snapshots the way AWS Backup does. Use CRR for object-level offsite copies and AWS Backup cross-Region copy for service-level recovery points.

How to

Configure cross-Region replication

Enable versioning on source and destination. Create a replication rule that specifies the destination bucket ARN and a role for replication. Optionally choose prefixes or tags to filter what replicates.
CLI reminder (concept)
aws s3api put-bucket-replication --bucket source-bucket --replication-configuration '{"Role": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/s3-replication-role", "Rules": [ { "ID": "CRR", "Status": "Enabled", "Destination": { "Bucket": "arn:aws:s3:::dest-bucket" } } ] }'

Replication is asynchronous. Verify replication by uploading a test file and checking the destination bucket. Account for storage and egress costs when replicating large datasets.
Key takeaway: CRR provides offsite object copies but does not replace multi-resource backup snapshots.
Common mistake: Forgetting to enable versioning on both buckets prevents replication from working as expected.

screens.title: Simulated Restore — validate recovery procedures
screens.narratorSegment: A simulated restore is the single most important validation for a backup strategy. It confirms that recovery points are usable, permissions are correct, and application components can be reconstructed. The typical simulated restore process has four steps. First, identify a recovery point: choose a specific backup snapshot or object version that meets your recovery criteria. Second, perform the restore into a dedicated test environment in your DR Region or test account; do not restore into production. Third, validate integrity: ensure databases start, application configuration files are correct, and that services can communicate with any dependent components. Fourth, document the process and update runbooks with any changes or surprises you encountered. A common misconception is that quick verification of file presence is enough; instead you must run the application or service to verify real recoverability. Practically, include timing measurements during tests so you understand actual RTOs. Record failures and corrective actions so the next test is faster and more reliable. Regular, scheduled simulated restores turn backups from a checkbox into a proven recovery capability. Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Simulated Restore
Four-step process

Identify → Restore → Validate → Document

  1. Identify a recovery point: choose a backup or object version that meets the RPO.
  2. Restore into a test environment: never validate by restoring into production.
  3. Validate integrity: run applications, check databases and dependencies.
  4. Document and update runbooks: capture timings and any fixes.
Example validation
Restore a database snapshot to a test DB instance, run application integration tests, and measure total time from restore start to fully functional service.
Common pitfalls
Assuming file presence equals usability without running the application.
Not measuring end-to-end restore time, which hides real RTO exposure.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › CLI Examples
Create a backup plan (example)
aws backup create-backup-plan \
  --backup-plan '{
    "BackupPlanName": "MyDailyBackupPlan",
    "Rules": [
      {
        "RuleName": "DailyRetention",
        "TargetBackupVaultName": "Default",
        "ScheduleExpression": "cron(0 5 ? * * *)",
        "StartWindowMinutes": 60,
        "CompletionWindowMinutes": 180,
        "Lifecycle": { "DeleteAfterDays": 35 },
        "CopyActions": [
          { "DestinationBackupVaultArn": "arn:aws:backup:us-west-2:123456789012:backup-vault:Default", "Lifecycle": { "DeleteAfterDays": 365 } }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }'
Assign resources (example)
aws backup put-backup-selection \
  --backup-plan-id "backup-plan-id-from-above" \
  --backup-selection '{
    "SelectionName": "MyApplicationResources",
    "IamRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/service-role/AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole",
    "Resources": [
      { "ResourceType": "EC2", "Conditions": { "StringEquals": { "ConditionKey": "Environment", "ConditionValue": "Production" } } },
      { "ResourceType": "RDS", "Conditions": { "StringEquals": { "ConditionKey": "Application", "ConditionValue": "WebApp" } } }
    ]
  }'
Validation
After running these commands, verify the backup vault and copied recovery points, then perform a test restore to confirm everything works.

screens.title: Common mistakes and pro-tips
screens.narratorSegment: In practice, a few recurring mistakes account for the majority of backup failures. First, incorrect IAM roles: AWS Backup and S3 replication require roles with explicit permissions to create snapshots, copy objects, and decrypt with KMS. Second, not testing restores: many teams assume backups are sufficient until a production incident reveals they are not restorable. Third, ignoring lifecycle and cost: keeping every recovery point indefinitely can become expensive, so define lifecycle transitions. Fourth, forgetting versioning or object lock on S3 buckets that hold critical configuration files; without versioning you cannot recover overwritten objects. Pro-tips to avoid these problems include automating backup-plan deployment in IaC so roles, vaults and lifecycle rules are versioned; scheduling regular simulated restores with pass/fail reporting; and documenting KMS key grants for cross-Region copies. Also, run a small-scale dry run of your plan in a non-production account to confirm IAM, KMS and replication behavior. A useful final check is to include timing metrics for restores in your runbook so stakeholders understand realistic recovery windows. These practices convert backups from an operational task to a proven recovery capability.

Top mistakes

  • Missing IAM or KMS permissions for backup and replication operations.

Document KMS grants and vault roles for cross-Region copies before a real outage.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how the Backup and Restore disaster recovery model uses managed backups and durable storage to protect data while keeping costs reasonable. We'll focus on AWS Backup as a centralized service that schedules, encrypts, and copies backups across Regions, and on Amazon S3 for storing durable objects with versioning and object lock. You will see practical configuration ideas: how to define backup rules, retention and lifecycle policies, assign resources by tag, and create cross-Region copies so that a catastrophic Region failure does not destroy your recovery points. We also cover S3 features like versioning and cross-Region replication to keep offsite object copies, and how to run a simulated restore to validate your runbook. A common risk to watch for is thinking a backup exists because a snapshot was taken; without the right IAM permissions, lifecycle rules, or tested restores, that backup may be unusable. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to design a backup plan that balances RTO and RPO needs, use S3 for durable offsite copies, and run a restore test to prove recovery. Consider what recovery time you can tolerate and how often you must copy backups to another Region before we begin.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure centralized backup plans, optimize retention and lifecycle to control cost, and use Amazon S3 features to protect object data. First, you'll define backup rules and vaults in AWS Backup so multiple services follow a single policy. Second, you'll implement schedules, retention and lifecycle to balance storage costs against recovery needs; this matters because long retention without lifecycle transitions increases expense. Third, you will enable S3 versioning and object lock so object histories are preserved and protected from accidental deletes or ransomware—this is essential for compliance and recovery. Lastly, you'll configure S3 Cross-Region Replication and AWS Backup cross-Region copy so recovery points are stored offsite. Each objective is practical: for example, assigning EC2 instances to a backup plan by tag ensures systems added later inherit the same protection automatically. A typical misconception is assuming a backup alone guarantees recovery; instead, you must test simulated restores and validate integrity. These skills let you design cost-effective, auditable backup policies that your team can rely on during a disaster. Which objective feels most urgent for your environment today?

This screen translates objectives into practical tasks you can perform. You'll create an AWS Backup plan with a daily schedule and retention policy, assign EC2 and RDS resources by tag, and add a cross-Region copy to a secondary Region. You'll also enable versioning on an S3 bucket and configure Cross-Region Replication, then upload and verify a sample object replicates. The reason these tasks matter is they translate policy into repeatable actions: tags ensure new instances are automatically backed up, replication keeps offsite copies without manual transfers, and test restores confirm that the whole system works. A common misconception is treating replication and backup as identical; replication is for object copies while AWS Backup handles snapshots and cross-Region backup copies at the service level. As you practice, pay attention to required IAM roles and encryption settings — both are common causes of failed backups or replication. These tasks will prepare you for the lab where you launch a small EC2, attach tags, create a backup plan, and verify cross-Region copies and S3 replication.

Backup and Restore is a disaster recovery model where you create recovery points in storage and restore systems and data only after an outage. It typically has longer recovery time objectives and recovery point objectives than warm standby or pilot light models, but it is often the most cost-efficient option for systems that can tolerate delays. Practically, this means you plan for longer downtime but benefit from lower ongoing costs because you do not maintain running standby infrastructure. For example, a non-critical batch processing application that runs once per day often uses Backup and Restore: nightly snapshots and S3 backups will let you recover within hours rather than minutes. A common misconception is assuming backups eliminate the need for testing. In reality, a backup is not useful unless you can restore it; therefore simulated restores and runbook validation are essential. Another contrast: replication and high-availability designs aim for minimal downtime, while Backup and Restore focuses on data durability and cost. The takeaway is to match recovery tolerances to business needs, and then design backup schedules, retention, and offsite copies to meet those tolerances while keeping costs under control. What recovery window does your application require, and does that match a Backup and Restore strategy?

AWS Backup is a fully managed service that centralizes backup operations across a range of AWS services. It supports EC2 snapshots, EBS volumes, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx and Storage Gateway volumes. Centralization matters because it frees teams from maintaining separate scripts for each service and enables consistent policy enforcement. For example, rather than creating separate retention scripts for each database, you define one backup plan with rules and apply it to all targets. This simplifies audits and enforces consistency. A typical setup includes a backup vault where snapshots are stored, often encrypted using a customer-managed key. You should be aware of roles: AWS Backup requires an IAM role with permissions to create snapshots and manage lifecycle; forgetting to attach the correct role is a common operational mistake. Another useful capability is copying backups to another Region automatically. This cross-Region copy is not the same as S3 replication; it's a managed copy of a backup recovery point. Finally, centralization also helps with reporting and compliance because backup activity appears in a single place. Practice: create a simple backup plan that targets EC2 and RDS to see these benefits play out in one policy.

Designing a backup plan starts with translating RTO and RPO into concrete rules: how often to take backups and how long to keep them. Begin by choosing a schedule expression that aligns with recovery point needs. For example, if you need hourly recovery points, schedule hourly backups; if daily is sufficient, choose a daily cron. Next, set a backup window that sets the preferred time to start backups to reduce load during peak hours. Then decide retention: short retention for frequent restores, longer retention for compliance. Finally, add lifecycle rules to transition older backups to colder storage for cost savings, such as moving snapshots to archival storage after thirty days. A cross-Region copy can be added as a copy action with its own retention to isolate recovery points. An example pattern is: daily backups, 7-day primary retention, cross-Region copy retained 30 days, and lifecycle transition to archive after 60 days. Remember a frequent mistake: setting very short start windows that cannot complete given the completion window — this can cause overlapping jobs. Validate your times against expected snapshot durations and adjust start and completion windows accordingly. The practical exercise is to convert your RTO/RPO requirements into these rule fields and test a manual restore.

Assigning resources by tag is a practical and scalable way to ensure new resources inherit backup protection. In AWS Backup, create a backup selection that targets specific resource types and includes conditions where a tag key equals a tag value, for example Environment equals Production. This minimizes manual selection and adapts to infrastructure that grows over time. Behind the scenes AWS Backup needs an IAM role that allows it to take snapshots and manage backups; the role must be provided in the backup selection call. A frequent operational pitfall is forgetting to set the IAM role in the selection, which prevents AWS Backup from accessing specified resources. Another consideration is resource type differences: some services, like RDS, have snapshot semantics different from EBS volume snapshots, so verify your selection covers the intended resource types. For example, assign EC2 and RDS resources to the same plan by specifying both resource types and the matching tag condition to ensure consistent retention. After assignment, trigger a manual run to confirm backups succeed and inspect the backup vault to confirm encryption and copy actions are present. This approach keeps policy enforcement declarative and repeatable.

A backup vault is a logical container where AWS Backup stores recovery points. Vaults are often encrypted using AWS KMS keys and are the primary boundary for access control and lifecycle management. Using vaults helps you separate environments or compliance categories; for instance you might store production backups in a vault with stricter encryption keys and longer retention. Lifecycle rules attached to backup rules let you transition backups to cheaper storage tiers after a period, reducing ongoing cost. For example, you can retain a snapshot in the primary vault for 35 days and then transition it to an archive tier or cross-Region copy retained for 365 days, depending on compliance needs. A common operational oversight is failing to set the correct KMS key grants for cross-Region copies—if the destination cannot decrypt, the copy will be unusable. Always validate encryption and IAM permissions for both the source and destination vaults. Finally, document vault usage and lifecycle policies so your team understands where to look for a recovery point, and automate reporting so that retention rules are enforced consistently. The core outcome is encrypted, auditable backup storage that also optimizes cost through lifecycle transitions.

Cross-Region copy in AWS Backup automatically copies a recovery point to a specified destination Region and backup vault. This protects against a Region-wide outage by keeping an independent, isolated copy of your backup outside the primary Region. You configure copy actions within a backup rule, specifying the destination vault ARN and lifecycle settings for the copy. Amazon S3 provides a durable and scalable object store suitable for storing backup data, logs, and configuration files. Its eleven nines of durability dramatically reduces the chance of object loss, making it a strong option for backup storage. Key S3 features for DR include versioning, which keeps multiple versions of an object so you can recover an earlier state after accidental deletion or overwrite. Object Lock provides write-once-read-many (WORM) protections to prevent deletion or modification for a defined retention period, which is valuable for regulatory compliance and ransomware protection. When using these features together you get both the ability to recover previous object versions and the assurance that a retention policy cannot be bypassed. However, enabling Object Lock and versioning requires planning because object lifecycles and replication behave differently when versions and locks are present. Cost is another factor: keeping many versions or large objects across Regions increases storage charges. Always balance protection needs against cost and operational complexity, and document S3 lifecycle, retention, and lock policies so teams understand how to recover object histories when needed. S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies objects from a source bucket in one AWS Region to a destination bucket in another Region. CRR is configured at the bucket level and requires versioning enabled on both source and destination buckets, plus an IAM role that allows replication. After enabling CRR, new objects and updates (when configured) are asynchronously replicated to the destination. This creates an offsite copy suitable for DR scenarios where object availability in another Region is needed. An example workflow is: enable versioning on both buckets, create the destination bucket, add a replication rule that targets all objects or a specific prefix, and create or grant the replication role. In practice, replication is not instantaneous; it is asynchronous and may take time depending on object size and throughput. Consider costs: storing replicated objects in another Region increases storage costs and potential egress on large-scale recovery. A common misconception is thinking replication replaces backups: replication copies objects but does not take consistent multi-resource snapshots the way AWS Backup does. Use CRR for object-level offsite copies and AWS Backup cross-Region copy for service-level recovery points.

A simulated restore is the single most important validation for a backup strategy. It confirms that recovery points are usable, permissions are correct, and application components can be reconstructed. The typical simulated restore process has four steps. First, identify a recovery point: choose a specific backup snapshot or object version that meets your recovery criteria. Second, perform the restore into a dedicated test environment in your DR Region or test account; do not restore into production. Third, validate integrity: ensure databases start, application configuration files are correct, and that services can communicate with any dependent components. Fourth, document the process and update runbooks with any changes or surprises you encountered. A common misconception is that quick verification of file presence is enough; instead you must run the application or service to verify real recoverability. Practically, include timing measurements during tests so you understand actual RTOs. Record failures and corrective actions so the next test is faster and more reliable. Regular, scheduled simulated restores turn backups from a checkbox into a proven recovery capability. In practice, a few recurring mistakes account for the majority of backup failures. First, incorrect IAM roles: AWS Backup and S3 replication require roles with explicit permissions to create snapshots, copy objects, and decrypt with KMS. Second, not testing restores: many teams assume backups are sufficient until a production incident reveals they are not restorable. Third, ignoring lifecycle and cost: keeping every recovery point indefinitely can become expensive, so define lifecycle transitions. Fourth, forgetting versioning or object lock on S3 buckets that hold critical configuration files; without versioning you cannot recover overwritten objects. Pro-tips to avoid these problems include automating backup-plan deployment in IaC so roles, vaults and lifecycle rules are versioned; scheduling regular simulated restores with pass/fail reporting; and documenting KMS key grants for cross-Region copies. Also, run a small-scale dry run of your plan in a non-production account to confirm IAM, KMS and replication behavior. A useful final check is to include timing metrics for restores in your runbook so stakeholders understand realistic recovery windows. These practices convert backups from an operational task to a proven recovery capability.

These are the essential concepts from the chapter. First, AWS Backup centralizes backups across many AWS services and supports backup plans, vaults, and cross-Region copies for service-level recovery points. Second, a backup plan is built from rules: schedule, start and completion windows, retention, lifecycle transitions, and copy actions. Third, backup vaults hold recovery points and should be encrypted with appropriate KMS keys and permissions. Fourth, Amazon S3 provides durable object storage; enable versioning to preserve object history and object lock for WORM protection. Fifth, S3 Cross-Region Replication gives offsite object copies but differs from AWS Backup's recovery-point copies. Finally, simulated restores are mandatory: identify a recovery point, restore to a test environment, validate integrity, and document the process. Keep these points in mind when designing a cost-effective DR strategy that balances protection, cost, and recovery time.

Keep three compact reminders in mind. First, centralize backup policies with AWS Backup to reduce operational complexity and enforce consistent retention and lifecycle across services. Second, protect S3 data with versioning and object lock and use Cross-Region Replication for offsite copies; understand CRR is for objects while AWS Backup handles recovery points. Third, always run simulated restores: identify a recovery point, restore into a test environment, validate application functionality, and update runbooks. These three practices—centralized policy, durable offsite copies, and validated restores—are the pillars of a reliable Backup and Restore disaster recovery approach. When you design or review a DR plan, ask if each pillar is present and demonstrable.
